vignette: Tane, sixty-three and of Oceania descent, sat in his study with his back resting lightly against the oak wall, his gaze fixed on the door. The trauma had begun three years earlier when a faulty valve in the publishing house’s upper archives ruptured, flooding the editing floors with a thick, chemical mist. The disaster was entirely man-made, born of rushed inspections and aging machinery, and what remains for him is not a blur but a series of sharp, unblinking photographs. He remembers the glint of shattering glass, the dark stain of industrial alcohol spreading across the concrete, and the way the emergency lights caught the dust hanging in the air. These visual memories are remarkably clear and detailed, and they force their way into his mind unbidden, usually dropping a perfect image into his thoughts during quiet moments or while he is reading a manuscript. He had come to believe that the event never truly ended; it simply waited for the right moment to surface. Mornings brought a heavy dream residue, as he would wake from a nightmare with the chemical mist still thick in his throat. He was certain that talking about the accident brought the past forward with startling precision, as if speaking its name summoned the scene into the room. The jumpy, alert feeling never fully settled. Even inside his own home, he felt on guard, his shoulders tightening at the slightest shift in the air. He jumped or startled at ordinary sounds—the microwave ding, a chair scraping against the floor, his wife’s footsteps in the hallway—as though his body had forgotten how to distinguish warning from routine. The startle response was immediate and physical, a quick bracing that arrived before his mind could catch up. The smell of alcohol on the radio or in a passing car’s exhaust accompanied a sharp recall of the chemical mist and the way it had coated his throat, so he stopped drinking at home. His PCL5 score of 79 mirrored the quiet intensity of these unbroken days. The avoidance habits formed quietly, accumulating over weeks and then months. Tane started scanning every room before he entered, his eyes tracking corners, doorways, and overhead fixtures for signs of something giving way. At dinner parties and industry gatherings, he consistently chose seats with his back pressed firmly against the wall, a posture that let him watch the room without being exposed. He avoided seeing friends. Their casual visits drew him into open spaces, and the jumpy feeling settled in. His work as a publisher intersected with these symptoms in concrete ways. During manuscript reviews, he would pace the perimeter of his home office, constantly checking the surroundings, his gaze sweeping over the stacks of galley proofs and the heavy bookshelf that lined the wall. When his editor called about a delayed deadline, Tane had to stop mid-stride to listen, his startle response flaring at the ring of his desk phone, while the visual memories of the disaster hovered just beneath the surface of his thoughts. His wife noticed how his avoidance had rippled into their daily routine. They stopped hosting book club evenings because he would leave early, citing a need to check the locks, and he declined weekend lunches with old college friends, preferring the predictable stillness of his own study. What frightened him most was not the event itself, but the certainty that the past could step forward without warning, that the alcohol scent or a sudden noise could pull him back into those photographs, and that the startle would continue to arrive uninvited. It was the cumulative weight of these days that finally brought Tane to seek help. He sat across from the therapist now, his hands folded tightly over his knees, his breathing measured but watchful. He had come to believe that the pictures would not fade on their own, and that without a way to steady his body’s responses, he would remain permanently braced against an ordinary world. He hoped to find a way to sit with his friends again, to let the startle pass without hijacking the moment, and to finally allow the past to remain in its place while he lived in the present.
